## Overview

How quickly does an infection recover from a treatment, how likely is it to
establish from a single infected cell, and does it warn before it collapses?
These are three simulation-based measures of resilience: the return rate
after a pulse, basin stability, and early-warning indicators. This vignette
measures all three on the viral front of @Capitan2011 (vignette 3) with
[DynamicalResilience.jl](https://github.com/ecorecipes/DynamicalResilience.jl).

DynamicalResilience drives a simulation through SciML's integrator interface,
whose methods `CellularAutomataCore` implements: `init`, `step!`, `reinit!`,
`set_u!`. So its measures apply to any problem in the zoo, and neither the zoo
nor the core depends on it.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using DynamicalResilience
using Plots
using Random
using Statistics
```

## A front with an exact threshold

Without mutation (`p = q = 0`) every virion keeps the ability `R`, and the
front is directed bond percolation: an infected cell infects each cell below
it unless all the virions it sends fail. Above the host resistance
`π_c = 0.3552998^(1/R)` the infection dies out (vignette 3). With `R = 2`,
`π_c ≈ 0.596`. A known threshold lets us check what each measure says as it
is approached.

```{julia}
const R = 2
πc = 0.3552998^(1 / R)
L = 2000
front(π; T=1200, seed=1, u0=fill(Int8(R), L)) =
    CAProblem(build(:domany_kinzel_viral; R), (r=u0,), T, (; π, p=0.0, q=0.0);
              space=Torus(L), seed)
round(πc; digits=4)
```

## Recovery after a treatment

At generation 200, when the front has settled, a treatment clears half of the
infected cells (`disturb!` from CellularAutomataCore). `recovery` runs the
front twice, with and without the treatment, and records the difference in the
density of infected cells. The two runs share their random numbers, before the
pulse because `reinit!` replays the run and after it because the core's random
numbers are keyed by seed, cell and generation. With `p = q = 0` an extra
infected cell can only make infection more likely, so the treated front stays
below the untreated one and eventually meets it. The return rate is the slope
of the logarithm of the difference.

```{julia}
treat(u, rng) = disturb!(copy(u), rng; fraction=0.5, from = >(0))
πs = [0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.54, 0.57, 0.585]
recoveries = Dict(π => [recovery(front(π; seed), Synchronous(); perturb=treat,
                                 observe=viral_density, t_pulse=200, horizon=1000,
                                 interval=1, rng=Xoshiro(seed), save_everystep=false)
                        for seed in 1:4]
                  for π in πs)
[(π=π, return_rate=round(median(r.return_rate for r in recoveries[π]); sigdigits=2),
  return_time=median(r.return_time for r in recoveries[π])) for π in πs]
```

```{julia}
fig1 = plot(; yscale=:log10, xlabel="generations after the treatment",
            ylabel="difference in density", legend=:topright, xlims=(0, 400),
            ylims=(1e-4, 1))
for (π, c) in ((0.45, 1), (0.54, 2), (0.585, 3))
    r = recoveries[π][2]
    keep = r.distance .> 0
    plot!(fig1, r.t[keep], r.distance[keep]; label="π = $π", color=c, lw=1.5)
end
fig2 = scatter(repeat(πs; inner=4), [x.return_rate for π in πs for x in recoveries[π]];
               xlabel="host resistance π", ylabel="return rate per generation",
               label="", ms=3)
vline!(fig2, [πc]; ls=:dash, color=:black, label="π_c")
plot(fig1, fig2; layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 360), left_margin=4Plots.mm,
     bottom_margin=5Plots.mm)
```

Far from the threshold the front recovers within about a dozen generations.
Approaching it, recovery slows sharply: the median return time grows from 12
generations at `π = 0.40` to a few hundred at `π = 0.585`, and the return rate
falls towards zero. This is critical slowing down, the slowing of recovery
near a critical point. The rates scatter more close to the threshold, where
the slow decay is easily interrupted by the moment the two fronts meet.

## Establishment from one infected cell

Basin stability asks how often a system ends in a given state from a random
start. Here the start is a single infected cell placed at random, and the
state is a front still infected after 2000 generations, with a ring of 1000
cells. Each trajectory has its own seed, through CellularAutomataCore's
`EnsembleProblem`:

```{julia}
one_cell(u, rng) = (v = zeros(Int8, length(u)); v[rand(rng, 1:length(u))] = Int8(R); v)
function establishment(π; n=300, L=1000, T=2000)
    base = CAProblem(build(:domany_kinzel_viral; R), (r=zeros(Int8, L),), T,
                     (; π, p=0.0, q=0.0); space=Torus(L), seed=1)
    ens = EnsembleProblem(base;
                          prob_func=(p, ctx) -> remake(p; seed=1000 + ctx.sim_id,
                                                       u0=one_cell(p.u0, Xoshiro(ctx.sim_id))),
                          output_func=(sol, ctx) -> (viral_density(sol.u[end]) > 0, false))
    alive = solve(ens, Synchronous(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories=n,
                  save_everystep=false).u
    p = mean(alive)
    return (π=π, established=round(p; digits=3), se=round(sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n); digits=3))
end
est = [establishment(π) for π in (0.50, 0.55, 0.58, 0.60, 0.62)]
```

A single infected cell establishes with probability 0.85 at `π = 0.50`, and
the probability falls steeply towards the threshold. Just above it a few
fronts are still alive after 2000 generations: at the critical point a front
dies out slowly, as a power of time, so the finite run overstates survival
there. By `π = 0.62` none survives.

DynamicalResilience's `basin_stability` builds its own ensemble, which sets
each trajectory's initial state but keeps the problem's seed. For a stochastic
cellular automaton every trajectory then shares one realisation of the noise:

```{julia}
shared = basin_stability(CAProblem(build(:domany_kinzel_viral; R), (r=zeros(Int8, 1000),),
                                   2000, (; π=0.60, p=0.0, q=0.0); space=Torus(1000), seed=1),
                         Synchronous(); sample_perturbation=one_cell, returned=x -> x > 0,
                         observe=viral_density, trajectories=300, seed=1,
                         save_everystep=false)
(shared_noise=round(shared.fraction; digits=3), se=round(shared.se; digits=3),
 independent=est[4].established)
```

The shared-noise estimate is a fraction for one realisation of the noise, not
the probability of establishment, and its binomial standard error does not
describe its error. Use independent seeds for stochastic models, as above.

## Early warnings along a slow ramp

Before the infection collapses, does the front warn? The resistance is raised
slowly from 0.40 to 0.62 over 3000 generations (`ramped_series` assigns
`integ.p`, which the core's integrator allows), and the density is recorded
every 2 generations. `early_warning` removes the trend and computes the
variance and the lag-1 autocorrelation in a moving window. Kendall's τ
measures whether they rise. The series stops 0.01 short of the threshold.
For comparison, the same calculation is run at a fixed `π = 0.45`:

```{julia}
T = 3000
function indicators(seed; ramp=true)
    r = ramp ? (p0, t) -> merge(p0, (; π=0.40 + 0.22 * t / T)) : nothing
    s = ramped_series(front(ramp ? 0.40 : 0.45; T, seed), Synchronous(); saveat=0:2:T,
                      ramp=r, observe=viral_density, save_everystep=false)
    πt = 0.40 .+ 0.22 .* s.t ./ T
    keep = findall(<(πc - 0.01), πt)
    return early_warning(s.x[keep]; t=s.t[keep], window=0.3, detrend=:gaussian,
                         bandwidth=0.1)
end
ews = Dict((seed, ramp) => indicators(seed; ramp) for seed in 1:4, ramp in (true, false))
[(seed=seed, ramp=ramp, τ_variance=round(ews[(seed, ramp)].tau_variance; digits=2),
  τ_ac1=round(ews[(seed, ramp)].tau_ac1; digits=2)) for ramp in (true, false) for seed in 1:4]
```

```{julia}
e = ews[(1, true)]
πw = 0.40 .+ 0.22 .* e.t ./ T
plot(plot(πw, e.variance; xlabel="host resistance π", ylabel="variance", label="", lw=1.5),
     plot(πw, e.ac1; xlabel="host resistance π", ylabel="lag-1 autocorrelation", label="",
          lw=1.5); layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 330), left_margin=4Plots.mm,
     bottom_margin=5Plots.mm)
```

Along the ramp the variance rises in every run, with τ close to 1, and the
autocorrelation rises too, though less consistently. At a fixed resistance τ
wanders on both sides of zero, so the signal is not an artefact of the
calculation. In directed percolation the fluctuations of the density and the
time they take to decay both grow near the threshold, which is what the two
indicators measure.

## Caveats

- **The model is the special case `p = q = 0`.** It is directed bond
  percolation, chosen because its threshold is known exactly. With mutation
  the threshold moves and has no closed form.
- **Finite ring and finite runs.** A ring of 1000 or 2000 cells and runs of a
  few thousand generations blur the threshold: survival just above it is
  overstated and the slowest recoveries are cut short.
- **Shared noise in `basin_stability`.** See above. The establishment
  probabilities in this vignette use independent seeds.
- **A slow ramp is still a ramp.** The early warnings are measured while the
  resistance changes, so the front never fully settles at any `π`.
